title: Digital Marketing in Rome: Getting Chosen in the City
description: In Rome the same business sells to residents and to people passing through. District, seasonality and reviews: what changes in getting found.
og_description: Two audiences, a district that counts for more than the city, and reviews that stand in for reputation: what works for getting chosen in Rome.
h1: Digital Marketing in Rome: Who Stays and Who Passes Through
hero_alt: White Cycladic architecture against a vivid blue sky
intro: Rome has one feature that changes how marketing works: the same business serves two audiences that look nothing alike. On one side the residents, who choose slowly and then stay for years. On the other, someone in the city for two days who decides in ten minutes. They search with different words, at different moments, and they are convinced by different signals.
Here is what changes in practice: why the district counts for more than the city, how Roman seasonality actually moves, and the work reviews do when the customer has never heard of you.

sections.h2: In Rome You Sell to Two Audiences on the Same Day
p: A resident chooses once and then stays. They look for a dentist, a plumber, a gym, they compare, they ask around, and the decision holds for years. Someone passing through does the opposite: they decide on the spot, almost always from a phone, often within a few hundred metres of where they are standing, and they will not be back.

The two search with different words. The resident searches for the service. The visitor searches for the service plus the location, and looks at the map before the website. Build all your communication around one of them and the other simply doesn't see you.
You don't have to pick one. You have to know which of the two brings more margin in your business, give that one the first line, and leave the other a route that still works.

sections.h2: The District Counts for More Than the City
p: Rome as a keyword says very little. The city is vast and has more than one centre: from the historic centre out to the Raccordo ring road the distances are such that you are dealing with separate markets, not with areas of the same one. People who are actually searching type the district: Prati, Trastevere, Monteverde, San Giovanni, EUR. That is where the competition sits, and the competition in Prati is not the competition in Centocelle.

If you have a physical location, that is good news, because the real catchment is smaller than it looks and you can hold it. A well kept Google Business Profile, with the district in the text and in the photos, does more work than a generic campaign across the whole city.

There is also a constraint that weighs more than distance in Rome: the traffic restrictions in the centre decide who can actually reach you by car, and at what time. It is worth writing that where people will see it, along with how to get there on public transport and where to park.

More than one location means treating them as separate businesses: a profile each, different photos, their own reviews. Merging them for convenience is the quickest way to show up poorly in both areas.

sections.h2: Roman Seasonality Doesn't Follow Everyone Else's Calendar
p: In a lot of Italian cities August is simply an empty month. Not in Rome, because the people who come from elsewhere come all year round and not in one season. The month does not empty out, it shifts: the residential districts lose people while the centre fills up. Sell to residents and you lose volume; sell to the people arriving and you gain it, often in the same week.

The same goes for long weekends, public holidays and the events that bring people into the city. A calendar built on the national average gets both sets of months wrong: the ones worth pushing on, and the ones where the budget is better left alone.
Checking it is simple: look at your own figures from last year, month by month, and line the campaigns up with the months that are good for you, not the ones that are good for the country.

sections.h2: For Someone Who Doesn't Know You, Reviews Are the Reputation
p: A resident can ask a neighbour. Someone who arrived yesterday has nobody to ask, so they read instead. For that audience reviews are not a side dish: they are the only evidence available before walking in.

The count matters, the date matters and the reply matters. Twenty recent reviews say more than eighty that stopped three years ago, because the real question is not whether you were good then but whether you are reliable now. And a well written reply to a bad review convinces more than plenty of good ones, because it shows how you handle a problem.
Asking for them is not begging. Ask right after the moment the customer is happiest, in person or by message, and make replying easy: a direct link, not instructions.

sections.h2: Social Talks to the Two Audiences in Different Ways
p: For a resident, social is memory: they see you, they recognise you, and when they need you they remember. For a visitor it is discovery: a video shot inside your place or in front of the window is often the first contact, and it reaches whoever happens to be nearby at that moment.
The content that works for both is also the cheapest to produce: show the place and the people. Not an advert, the place. Real photos do the job word of mouth usually does.

One thing has to hold: the profile has to say where you are, what your hours are, and what happens if someone writes. A well kept profile that never answers direct messages loses exactly the enquiries it generated.

sections.h2: Do You Need an Agency Based in Rome?
p: Not necessarily. We work remotely, with our operations base in Durrës and a team that writes and calls in Italian. What counts is who knows your market and who answers when an enquiry lands, not the distance in kilometres.
That said, knowledge of a district cannot be improvised and is not in any tool. It is the part the client already has, and the part the agency has to be told at the start, before writing a line.
We work with businesses in Italy, Switzerland, the rest of Europe and the United States, and every enquiry is called and qualified before it reaches the client.

summary: In Rome you serve two audiences: residents choose slowly, visitors decide in minutes.
Competition happens at district level: hold your area, not the whole city.
Local seasonality doesn't match the national one: look at your own figures, not the calendar.
For someone who doesn't know you, recent reviews are the only evidence available.
Social is memory for residents and discovery for people passing through.

faq.q: Is it better to target all of Rome or one district?
faq.a: If you have a physical location, the district and the areas next to it. People don't travel far for a local service, so the real catchment is narrow, and putting budget and content there costs less and returns more than covering a city where most people would never come to you anyway.

faq.q: Is it worth communicating in English as well?
faq.a: It depends on how much of your revenue comes from people passing through. If it is a significant share, at least the essential information should be readable in English: what you do, where you are, the hours and how to book. Translating the whole site is a later step, decided on the numbers.

faq.q: How do you handle the August drop?
faq.a: First by checking there really is one: in Rome it depends on the area and the type of customer, and for some businesses August is a busy month. If the drop is real, it is the moment to spend less on acquisition and use the time for the things that never get done in the other months, from the photos to the Google profile to the reviews.
